clue.text: Dorothy Wordsworth's best-loved flower

explanation.surface: A literary question about which bloom the diarist Dorothy Wordsworth loved most.
explanation.walkthrough: Dorothy Wordsworth's best-loved person was her brother, the poet William, so the first sense is her dear William; the second is the garden plant of the pink family.
explanation.definitionFit: Dorothy adored her brother William, the poet, and the same two words name a cottage-garden pink with clustered blooms.

clue.text: Hold up, Susan, it is staggering

indicators.note: staggering means reeling unsteadily, so the letters of Susan and it lurch into a new order

explanation.surface: A bystander asks Susan to stop, since she is walking unsteadily.
explanation.definitionFit: To support something or keep it going is to bear its weight and maintain it.

clue.text: George lived near Lewes

parts.note: Lewes is a town in Sussex, but also the surname of George Henry Lewes, partner of the novelist who wrote as George

explanation.surface: A biographical note that a man called George lived close to the Sussex town of Lewes.
explanation.walkthrough: Lewes reads as the Sussex county town; really it is George Henry Lewes, with whom the novelist Mary Ann Evans, writing as George, lived for over twenty years.
explanation.definitionFit: The Victorian novelist Mary Ann Evans wrote under a male pen name and lived with the critic G H Lewes.

clue.text: Striking power of a Hans Andersen story

explanation.surface: The dramatic force of one of Hans Christian Andersen's fairy tales.
explanation.walkthrough: Before matches, a striking kit of flint and steel was kept with dry kindling in a box; Andersen's tale has a soldier find a magic one.
explanation.definitionFit: It held flint, steel and kindling for striking a light, and gives its name to an Andersen fairy tale about a soldier.

clue.text: French battle village takes nothing from the African coast

indicators.note: takes ... from says one piece is removed from the other, here the nought out of the coast
from goes with takes: the nought is taken out of the name of the coast

parts.note: the Ivory Coast is a country on the west African coast
O, the figure nought, stands for nothing

explanation.surface: A French village where a battle was fought borrows nothing from the coast of Africa.
explanation.walkthrough: Remove O from IVORY. Henri IV of France won the Battle of Ivry in 1590.
explanation.definitionFit: Ivry-la-Bataille in Normandy was the site of a 1590 victory by Henri IV over the Catholic League.

clue.text: She became a piquant columnist

parts.note: a columnist usually writes a newspaper column, but here she literally became a pillar, a salty and so piquant one

explanation.surface: A woman who took up writing a sharp, spicy newspaper column.
explanation.walkthrough: In Genesis, the wife of Lot looked back at Sodom and was turned into a pillar of salt: a column, and salty, so piquant.
explanation.definitionFit: The Bible says this woman was turned into a pillar of salt for looking back at the burning city of Sodom.

clue.text: A pretty smart girl lived in this way

definitions.text: A pretty smart girl lived in this way

parts.words: A pretty smart girl lived in this way
parts.note: recalls the old song Sally in our ..., whose heroine is the smartest of girls and lives in a narrow lane

explanation.surface: A rather clever young woman lived her life in a certain manner.
explanation.walkthrough: Way reads as manner, but it is a street; pretty smart reads as rather clever, but the song calls Sally the smartest girl of all.
explanation.definitionFit: Sally in the old ballad lives in a narrow passage between buildings, a back lane.

clue.text: Sligo shoes ?

parts.note: Sligo, an Irish county town, is read as sly go: shoes for going slyly, soft-soled for creeping about

explanation.surface: A question about footwear from Sligo in the west of Ireland.
explanation.walkthrough: Sligo is a town and county in the west of Ireland; said as sly go it describes the silent creeping that soft rubber-soled shoes allow.
explanation.definitionFit: Soft-soled canvas shoes let the wearer creep about quietly and stealthily, which earned them the name.

clue.text: Herbert (like his friend with expectations) was often out of it

definitions.text: Herbert (like his friend with expectations) was often out of it

parts.words: Herbert (like his friend with expectations) was often out of it
parts.note: Herbert is Pip's friend in Great Expectations, and both young men were often short of money, out of funds

explanation.surface: A man called Herbert, like his hopeful friend, was frequently dazed.
explanation.walkthrough: Out of it reads as dazed, but the phrase is out of pocket, short of money. Herbert's surname in Dickens's Great Expectations is the same word, and Pip is the friend with expectations.
explanation.definitionFit: Herbert's surname in Dickens is also the purse or pouch where money is carried; to be out of it is to be broke.

clue.text: Spider's little Jenny?

parts.note: a spinning jenny is a spinning machine; a small spinner with the diminutive ending -et is the organ a spider spins its silk from

explanation.surface: A spider's tiny female companion called Jenny.
explanation.walkthrough: Jenny looks like a pet name, but a spinning jenny is a machine for spinning thread, and the spider's own little spinner is its silk gland.
explanation.definitionFit: The silk-producing organ at the rear of a spider is a small spinning device, as a spinning jenny is a large one.

clue.text: When Colin lacks firm permission to proceed, there's language

indicators.note: the man's name is said to be without the firm, so those letters are taken out of it

parts.note: CO is the usual abbreviation for company, a firm
to give the go is to give permission to proceed

explanation.surface: Once Colin no longer has the company's approval to go ahead, people start talking.
explanation.walkthrough: Take CO from COLIN to leave LIN, then add GO.
explanation.definitionFit: Lingo is informal slang for a language or jargon, especially one foreign or unfamiliar to the speaker.

clue.text: Headwear that preceded the deerstalker

parts.note: the deerstalker hat is named after the hunter, but the deer itself wore its branched horns on its head before any hunter came

explanation.surface: A question of hat history: what people wore before the deerstalker came into fashion.
explanation.walkthrough: The deerstalker reads as the hat Sherlock Holmes wears; here the stag carried its headgear before the man who stalks it did.
explanation.definitionFit: A stag's branched horn grows on its head, a natural headpiece worn long before any hunting cap.

clue.text: Middling-depressed by clue for "yaws"

parts.note: the word yaws is the word sway spelt backwards, so a clue for it could be ...

explanation.surface: A medical-sounding note about someone sunk in the middle, next to a clue for a tropical disease.
explanation.walkthrough: Yaws is a tropical skin disease; its letters are SWAY written back to front. Middling-depressed describes a horse whose back sags in the middle.
explanation.definitionFit: A horse with this condition has a spine that dips abnormally in its middle, so it is sunk at the midpoint.

clue.text: It's not far, Barney, pull yourself together

indicators.note: Barney is told to reassemble himself, so his name's letters are rearranged into a new form

explanation.surface: Someone tells a flustered Barney to compose himself, since the place they want is close.
explanation.definitionFit: Something close at hand, a short distance away, is described as being in the vicinity.

clue.text: The whole time some Widdicombe leeway

explanation.surface: Someone was allowed a little slack at Widdicombe throughout.
explanation.walkthrough: The Devon folk song Widecombe Fair has the refrain 'All along, down along, out along lee', so a piece of its 'lee' way is these two words.
explanation.definitionFit: Throughout or from the start means continuously, and the phrase also opens the refrain of the Widecombe Fair song.

clue.text: A noisy speakeasy, prosperous

indicators.note: a noisy word is one meant to be heard, so the word for speakeasy is taken by its sound

parts.note: split as speak easy, someone who speaks easily is fluent

explanation.surface: A loud illicit drinking den is doing very well for itself.
explanation.walkthrough: A speakeasy is a Prohibition-era illegal bar, but split it into speak easy: one who does so is FLUENT, and A FLUENT said out loud gives the answer.
explanation.definitionFit: Wealthy people who are doing well financially are well off, rich and flourishing.

clue.text: Victor's wearing leaves much to be desired

definitions.text: Victor's wearing leaves much to be desired

parts.words: Victor's wearing leaves much to be desired
parts.note: leaves much to be desired normally means poor, but here a winner wearing a wreath of bay leaves is in a state much desired

explanation.surface: The winner's outfit is disappointing.
explanation.walkthrough: The idiom 'leaves much to be desired' suggests the outfit is poor; read literally, the victor wears a crown of bay leaves, and to be so crowned is much to be desired.
explanation.definitionFit: A victor in ancient games was crowned with a wreath of bay leaves, the traditional sign of honour.

clue.text: Not perhaps the G.I.'s favourite flower

definitions.text: Not perhaps the G.I.'s favourite flower

parts.words: Not perhaps the G.I.'s favourite flower
parts.note: a white spring flower whose name was Second World War slang for an American military policeman, so hardly loved by ordinary soldiers

explanation.surface: A remark on which bloom American soldiers might like least.
explanation.walkthrough: American military police wore white helmets, gloves and belts and were nicknamed after the white flower; GIs, the private soldiers they policed, had little love for them.
explanation.definitionFit: The small white early-spring bloom gave its name to US military policemen in white helmets, unpopular with ordinary soldiers.

clue.text: In slacks of course, minus braces

definitions.text: In slacks of course, minus braces

parts.words: In slacks of course, minus braces
parts.note: slacks are loose trousers, and taking off the braces that hold them up lets them loosen; both describe taking it easy

explanation.surface: A fashion note on wearing loose trousers without braces holding them up.
explanation.walkthrough: To slack is to loosen, and a man in slacks with no braces is loosened up and at ease. Braces are what Americans call suspenders.
explanation.definitionFit: Unwinding and taking one's ease is a loosening of tension, like trousers with nothing holding them taut.

clue.text: Fu' and stagger round to take in more

indicators.note: the word for stagger goes round, enclosing the clue's Fu' inside it

parts.note: to reel is to stagger unsteadily
Fu' is given as written, the Scots spelling of full meaning drunk

explanation.surface: A drunk Scot staggering about and then going for another drink.
explanation.walkthrough: Fu' is Scots for full, meaning drunk, which fits the surface's tipsy Scot; 'round' signals that it goes inside the word for stagger.
explanation.definitionFit: Filling up a vehicle's tank again with petrol is taking on a fresh supply of fuel.

clue.text: Kisses for conductors, say ?

explanation.surface: Someone blows kisses to the conductors.
explanation.walkthrough: To buss is an old word for to kiss; busses is also an old plural of bus, the vehicle a bus conductor worked on.
explanation.definitionFit: A buss is a smacking kiss, and the alternative plural of the public vehicle names where ticket collectors worked.

clue.text: Nobody to be seen

parts.note: normally means the place is empty, but read as no body to be seen it describes a bodiless figure that is nonetheless seen

explanation.surface: Someone looks around and finds the place empty.
explanation.walkthrough: Read 'Nobody' as 'no body': a ghost is a visible figure with no physical body.
explanation.definitionFit: A ghost or apparition is a form that appears to the eye but has no material body.

clue.text: How Jack was hurt from two heights

parts.note: a fell is a hill or high moor in northern England
a down is a rolling chalk hill, as in the South Downs of southern England

explanation.surface: An account of how someone called Jack injured himself in a fall from some height.
explanation.walkthrough: In the nursery rhyme Jack and Jill, Jack fell down and broke his crown. A fell is a northern English hill and the downs are southern English chalk hills.
explanation.definitionFit: The rhyme says Jack tumbled and broke his crown, so he was injured by toppling over.

clue.text: The courage needed to go into Europe?

definitions.text: The courage needed to go into Europe?

parts.words: The courage needed to go into Europe?
parts.note: courage from drink is called by a nationality's name, and the same nationality belongs to a country of Europe

explanation.surface: A question about the nerve Britain needed to join the European Community.
explanation.walkthrough: Dutch courage is the boldness that comes from drinking alcohol, and the Netherlands is a European country; Britain was then joining the Common Market.
explanation.definitionFit: Courage from drink is named after the people of the Netherlands, a country on the European mainland.

clue.text: Fanny by footlight

parts.note: plays on the film title Fanny by Gaslight, pointing to a Fanny who appeared under stage footlights

explanation.surface: A take on the period film Fanny by Gaslight, with stage lighting instead.
explanation.walkthrough: Fanny Kemble was a celebrated English stage actress of the 1830s, from a famous theatrical family, so she was seen by the footlights at the front of a stage.
explanation.definitionFit: The surname belongs to Fanny, a Victorian actress who performed in front of theatre footlights.

clue.text: By radio signal a note to Sir Robert to return

parts.note: B is a note of the musical scale

indicators.note: to return means the statesman's surname is turned round and read backwards

parts.note: Sir Robert Peel was a British prime minister and founder of the London police

explanation.surface: A message sent by radio to a statesman called Sir Robert, asking him to come back.
explanation.walkthrough: Sir Robert Peel was the 19th-century British prime minister who founded the Metropolitan Police; 'to return' turns his surname round, after the note.
explanation.definitionFit: A short high electronic tone sent by a radio device is a beep or electronic pip.

clue.text: A measure of port

explanation.surface: A glass of port wine poured out.
explanation.walkthrough: Port reads as the fortified wine, but it is a harbour town: Acre on the coast of northern Israel.
explanation.definitionFit: A unit of land area of 4,840 square yards, and an ancient harbour city on the coast of Israel.

clue.text: Teuton in a way stern

indicators.note: in a way says the word stern is only loosely itself, its letters reorganised into a new order

explanation.surface: A German who is rather severe in manner.
explanation.walkthrough: Max Ernst was a German surrealist painter, and Ernst is also a common German first name.
explanation.definitionFit: Ernst is a typically German forename, so a man of that name stands for a German.

clue.text: Rally the scattered, mind

explanation.surface: An appeal to gather the dispersed, and to remember it.
explanation.walkthrough: Split as re-collect, it means gather together again; as one word it means call to mind.
explanation.definitionFit: To gather again those who have dispersed, and to bring a memory back into the head, as in remember.

clue.text: That's dished you, pastor

parts.note: dished means served on a plate, and a pastor is literally a shepherd of his flock, so this is the dish belonging to such a man

explanation.surface: Someone gloats to a clergyman that he has been defeated.
explanation.walkthrough: To dish someone is to ruin them, but dished here means served up; pastor is Latin for shepherd, and the minced-lamb dish with mashed potato topping is his.
explanation.definitionFit: A minced meat dish under mashed potato is named after a herdsman, and a pastor is a herdsman of souls.
